papers.title: H1N1 preimmunity improves antibody responses to vaccination and alters draining lymph node germinal center signatures
papers.abstract: Influenza viruses circulate annually in humans, accumulating mutations in the viral genome. In real-world conditions, people develop an immune history from multiple influenza virus infections and vaccinations, yet most experimental studies utilize naïve hosts to investigate viral pathogenesis or vaccine efficacy; a scenario that does not reflect actual human exposure and immune responses. Here, we report that mice previously infected with the mouse-adapted H1N1 virus mounted an increased antibody response after vaccination with the split virion quadrivalent seasonal influenza vaccine. Antibodies targeting the H1 antigen component of the vaccine in H1N1 preimmune mice had titers peaking at a log 2 HAI titer of 8 versus 2 in naïve-vaccinated mice at 14 days post-vaccination, whereas H3N2 pre-immune mice showed no improved vaccine responses. Increased total serum class-switched IgG subclass concentrations in the H1N1 preimmune-vaccinated mice accompanied protection from weight loss and mortality when these mice were challenged with an H1N1 pandemic 2009 strain. Temporal sampling and analysis of RNA from mediastinal lymph nodes from preimmune mice by RNA-seq at time points following vaccination revealed distinct regulation of lymphocyte and germinal center-specific genes, including Bcl6 , an essential gene for germinal-center-dependent B-cells. Taken together, H1N1 A/FM/1/1947 preimmunity led to a more efficient vaccine response accompanied by altered expression of germinal center-associated genes in the mediastinal lymph node, with implications for future vaccine design.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza viruses circulate annually in humans, accumulating mutations in the viral genome. The study aimed to investigate how prior immunity to H1N1 affects vaccine responses in real-world conditions.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved mice previously infected with the mouse-adapted H1N1 virus and compared their responses to vaccination with naïve mice. It was conducted in a controlled laboratory setting using mice as the host.
analysis.methods: The researchers vaccinated mice with the split virion quadrivalent seasonal influenza vaccine and measured antibody titers against the H1 antigen. They also analyzed RNA from mediastinal lymph nodes using RNA-seq to assess gene expression changes.
analysis.main_results: H1N1 preimmune mice exhibited higher antibody titers against the H1 antigen, peaking at a log 2 HAI titer of 8 compared to 2 in naïve-vaccinated mice at 14 days post-vaccination. H3N2 pre-immune mice showed no improved vaccine responses. Increased total serum class-switched IgG subclass concentrations in H1N1 preimmune-vaccinated mice were observed.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that prior H1N1 infection enhances vaccine efficacy by increasing antibody titers and altering germinal center gene expression, which may inform future vaccine design.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results have implications for understanding how preexisting immunity influences vaccine effectiveness, potentially guiding the development of more efficient influenza vaccines.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study used mice as a model, which may not fully reflect human immune responses. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on animal models and does not include human data.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates how prior immunity to H1N1 influences vaccine responses in mice. It reports that H1N1 preimmune mice showed increased antibody titers and altered germinal center gene expression after vaccination, suggesting potential implications for vaccine design. The study used a mouse model and compared vaccinated preimmune and naïve mice. While the results are promising, the findings are limited to animal models and do not include human data, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 流感病毒在人类中每年循环传播,积累突变于病毒基因组中。本研究旨在探讨在现实条件下,先前对H1N1的免疫力如何影响疫苗反应。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究涉及先前感染过鼠源适应型H1N1病毒的小鼠,并将其与未感染小鼠进行比较,以评估其对疫苗接种的反应。研究在受控的实验室环境中进行,使用小鼠作为宿主。
elements_zh.methods: 研究人员使用四价裂解病毒颗粒季节性流感 疫苗对小鼠进行疫苗接种,并测量其对H1抗原的抗体滴度。他们还通过RNA测序分析纵隔淋巴结中的RNA,以评估基因表达的变化。
elements_zh.main_results: H1N1前免疫小鼠对H1抗原的抗体滴度更高,在接种疫苗接种后14天达到log 2 HAI滴度8,而未感染接种小鼠的滴度仅为2。H3N2前免疫小鼠未表现出改善的疫苗反应。在H1N1前免疫接种小鼠中,观察到总血清类转换IgG亚类浓度增加。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些发现表明,先前的H1N1感染通过增加抗体滴度和改变生发中心基因表达来增强疫苗的效果,这可能为未来疫苗的设计提供参考。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果有助于理解先前免疫力如何影响疫苗的效果,可能指导开发更有效的流感疫苗。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究使用小鼠作为模型,这可能无法完全反映人类免疫应答。由于基于动物模型且未包括人类数据,证据强度中等。

papers.abstract_zh: 流感病毒在人类中每年循环传播,积累突变于病毒基因组中。在现实条件下,人们通过多次流感病毒感染和疫苗接种形成免疫历史,但大多数实验研究使用未感染的宿主来研究病毒发病机制或疫苗的效果;这种情景无法反映实际的人类暴露和免疫应答。在这里,我们报告称,先前感染过鼠源适应型H1N1病毒的小鼠在接种疫苗接种后,对四价裂解病毒颗粒季节性流感 疫苗的抗体反应增强。在H1N1前免疫小鼠中,针对疫苗中H1抗原组分的抗体滴度在接种疫苗接种后14天达到log 2 HAI滴度8,而未感染接种小鼠的滴度仅为2。相比之下,H3N2前免疫小鼠未表现出改善的疫苗反应。在H1N1前免疫接种小鼠中,总血清类转换IgG亚类浓度增加,这些小鼠在被H1N1大流行2009株感染时表现出对体重减轻和死亡率的保护作用。通过在接种疫苗接种后不同时间点对前免疫小鼠的纵隔淋巴结进行RNA测序分析,研究人员发现淋巴细胞和生发中心特异性基因的调控存在显著差异,包括Bcl6,这是依赖生发中心的B细胞的关键基因。综上所述,H1N1 A/FM/1/1947前免疫导致了更有效的疫苗反应,并伴随纵隔淋巴结中与生发中心相关的基因表达改变,这可能对未来疫苗的设计产生影响。

papers.title: INFLUENZA VIRUS CIRCULATION DURING 2024-2025 SEASON IN RABAT, MOROCCO
papers.abstract: Introduction: Influenza remains a major cause of respiratory morbidity worldwide. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that seasonal influenza epidemic is responsible for millions of severe infections and hundreds of thousands of deaths each year. Global surveillance of influenza viruses is coordinated via the World Health Organization Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS). The organization follows circulating influenza virus on all continents and provides relevant information for vaccine strain selection as well as public health considerations. This study describes the circulation patterns of influenza viruses at Mohammed V Military Teaching Hospital (MVMTH) in Rabat during the 2024-2025 Influenza season. Methods: A prospective observational study was conducted from October 2024 to March 2025. Nasopharyngeal swabs from patients with influenza-like illness were analyzed using RT-PCR (Film Array Respiratory Panel and GeneXpert Xpress Flu/RSV). Results: Influenza A viruses showed up in most of the tested samples. Among influenza A viruses, viral A(H1N1)pdm09 infection was detected the most commonly. Influenza B viruses were also recorded but circulated at lower levels during the surveillance period. One hundred and sixteen cases were confirmed. Influenza A predominated (80%; n=93), while Influenza B accounted for 20% (n=23). Among Type A cases, A(H1N1)pd2009 was the primary subtype identified (64.5%; n=60), followed by non-subtyped strains (35.5%; n=33). A(H3N2) circulation was marginal (2.8%). Temporally, A(H1N1) peaked in week 4 of 2025, whereas Influenza B showed dominant activity in the late season (Weeks 14-17). Conclusion: The 2024-2025 season was characterized by the dominance of Influenza A(H1N1) and a late-season shift to Influenza B. These findings highlight the necessity of local surveillance to optimize hospital resource allocation and vaccination timing in Morocco.
papers.journal: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews

This study describes the circulation patterns of influenza viruses at Mohammed V Military Teaching Hospital (MVMTH) in Rabat during the 2024-2025 Influenza season. Methods: A prospective observational study was conducted from October 2024 to March 2025. Nasopharyngeal swabs from patients with influenza-like illness were analyzed using RT-PCR (Film Array Respiratory Panel and GeneXpert Xpress Flu/RSV). Results: Influenza A viruses showed up in most of the tested samples. Among influenza A viruses, viral A(H1N1)pdm09 infection was detected the most commonly. Influenza B viruses were also recorded but circulated at lower levels during the surveillance period. One hundred and sixteen cases were confirmed. Influenza A predominated (80%; n=93), while Influenza B accounted for 20% (n=23). Among Type A cases, A(H1N1)pd2009 was the primary subtype identified (64.5%; n=60), followed by non-subtyped strains (35.5%; n=33). A(H3N2) circulation was marginal (2.8%). Conclusion: The 2024-2025 season was characterized by the dominance of Influenza A(H1N1) and a late-season shift to Influenza B. These findings highlight the necessity of local surveillance to optimize hospital resource allocation and vaccination timing in Morocco.

papers.title: Antigenic and structural analysis of the influenza hemagglutinin lateral patch
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The lateral patch epitope of the H1 hemagglutinin (HA) was a dominant target of antibodies following exposure to the 2009 pandemic H1N1 virus. However, the conservation and mechanisms of antigenic drift in the lateral patch remain unresolved. Here, we used lateral patch-specific monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) to understand the antigenicity of the lateral patch of human, avian, and swine H1N x viruses spanning from 1918 to 2022. We found that lateral patch-specific mAbs demonstrated broad binding to pre-2009 H1N1 viruses and to the pandemic 2009 H1N1. However, we identified discrete mutations that drove multiple antibody evasion pathways for lateral patch-targeting mAbs in post-2009 H1N1 viruses. Despite this, we observed that the lateral patch remains well conserved across enzootic sources, suggesting that existing lateral patch antibodies could protect against a future zoonotic H1N x pandemic. Together, these data support that the lateral patch remains an attractive target for pandemic preparedness against emergent H1N x viruses. IMPORTANCE Seasonal influenza viruses continually undergo antigenic drift to evade antibody-mediated immunity, yet how individual antibody specificities shape this evolution remains poorly understood. We investigated the conservation and antigenic evolution of the H1 hemagglutinin (HA) lateral patch, an epitope targeted by broadly neutralizing antibodies. Using human monoclonal antibodies, we found that the lateral patch had remained highly conserved across nearly a century of human and animal influenza virus circulation but has undergone antigenic drift multiple times in pre- and post-2009 seasonal H1N1 viruses. Structural and mutational analyses revealed how these substitutions alter antibody recognition and shape the genetic features of lateral patch-targeting antibodies across individuals born in different eras. The lateral patch is also conserved among swine and avian H1N x viruses, highlighting its potential as a target of protective immunity against pandemic H1N x viruses. These findings provide a comprehensive framework for understanding antibody-driven evolution within a broadly conserved influenza virus epitope.

papers.title_zh: 甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09血凝素侧翼抗原表位的抗原性和结构分析
papers.source_body_en: ABSTRACT The lateral patch epitope of the H1 hemagglutinin (HA) was a dominant target of antibodies following exposure to the 2009 pandemic H1N1 virus. However, the conservation and mechanisms of antigenic drift in the lateral patch remain unresolved. Here, we used lateral patch-specific monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) to understand the antigenicity of the lateral patch of human, avian, and swine H1N x viruses spanning from 1918 to 2022. We found that lateral patch-specific mAbs demonstrated broad binding to pre-2009 H1N1 viruses and to the pandemic 2009 H1N1. However, we identified discrete mutations that drove multiple antibody evasion pathways for lateral patch-targeting mAbs in post-2009 H1N1 viruses. Despite this, we observed that the lateral patch remains well conserved across enzootic sources, suggesting that existing lateral patch antibodies could protect against a future zoonotic H1N x pandemic. Together, these data support that the lateral patch remains an attractive target for pandemic preparedness against emergent H1N x viruses. IMPORTANCE Seasonal influenza viruses continually undergo antigenic drift to evade antibody-mediated immunity, yet how individual antibody specificities shape this evolution remains poorly understood. We investigated the conservation and antigenic evolution of the H1 hemagglutinin (HA) lateral patch, an epitope targeted by broadly neutralizing antibodies. Using human monoclonal antibodies, we found that the lateral patch had remained highly conserved across nearly a century of human and animal influenza virus circulation but has undergone antigenic drift multiple times in pre- and post-2009 seasonal H1N1 viruses. Structural and mutational analyses revealed how these substitutions alter antibody recognition and shape the genetic features of lateral patch-targeting antibodies across individuals born in different eras. The lateral patch is also conserved among swine and avian H1N x viruses, highlighting its potential as a target of protective immunity against pandemic H1N x viruses. These findings provide a comprehensive framework for understanding antibody-driven evolution within a broadly conserved influenza virus epitope.
papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09的侧翼表位是抗体在接触2009年大流行H1N1病毒后的主要靶标。然而,该侧翼区域中抗原漂移的保守性和机制仍未明确。在此研究中,我们使用针对侧翼区域的单克隆抗体(mAbs)来分析1918年至2022年间人类、禽类和猪类H1N x病毒的侧翼区域抗原性。我们发现,针对侧翼区域的单克隆抗体在预2009年H1N1病毒和2009年大流行H1N1病毒中均表现出广泛的结合能力。然而,我们识别出一些离散的突变,这些变化驱动了针对侧翼区域的单克隆抗体的多种逃逸途径。尽管如此,我们观察到侧翼区域在流行性来源中仍然高度保守,这表明现有的侧翼区域抗体可能能够保护人类免受未来人兽共患病H1N x病毒的侵袭。综上所述,这些数据支持侧翼区域作为应对新兴H1N x病毒大流行的有吸引力的靶标。重要性 人兽共患病病毒持续经历抗原漂移以逃避抗体介导的免疫反应,但个体抗体特异性如何塑造这种抗原漂移仍不明确。我们研究了H1血凝素(HA)侧翼区域的保守性和抗原性漂移,该区域是广泛中和抗体的靶标。通过使用人类单克隆抗体,我们发现侧翼区域在近一个世纪的人类和动物流感病毒传播中保持高度保守,但在2009年前后季节性H1N1病毒中经历了多次抗原漂移。结构和突变分析揭示了这些替换如何改变抗体识别能力,并塑造不同年代个体中针对侧翼区域的抗体的遗传特征。此外,侧翼区域在猪类和禽类H1N x病毒中也保持保守,突显其作为针对大流行H1N x病毒保护性免疫靶标的潜力。这些发现为理解在广泛保守的流感病毒表位中抗体驱动的抗原漂移提供了全面的框架。

papers.title: Influenza Virus Antigenic Drift: Balancing Fitness and Immune Evasion
papers.abstract: Human influenza viruses demonstrate immense antigenic variability as a strategy to evade host immunity. The process of evolving to evade host antibody responses, known as antigenic drift, allows influenza viruses to evade epitope-specific antibodies, leading to seasonal influenza outbreaks. Neutralizing antibodies, the major drivers of antigenic drift, target a wide range of epitopes in hemagglutinin and neuraminidase, including functionally conserved regions. In this review, we describe antibody targets of influenza viruses, how influenza viruses have evolved to evade these antibody specificities, and how epistasis helps maintain viral fitness. Then we discuss emerging approaches to study and predict antigenic drift that may improve strain selection for seasonal influenza vaccines.

papers.abstract_zh: 人类流感病毒通过巨大的抗原变异作为策略来逃避宿主免疫。进化以逃避宿主抗体反应的过程,称为抗原漂移,使流感病毒能够逃避表位特异性抗体,导致季节性流感 暴发。中和抗体是抗原漂移的主要驱动力,它们针对血凝素和神经氨酸酶中的多种表位,包括功能保守区域。在本综述中,我们描述了流感病毒的抗体靶点,流感病毒如何进化以逃避这些抗体特异性,以及表型互作如何帮助维持病毒适应性。然后我们讨论了研究和预测抗原漂移的新方法,这些方法可能有助于改进季节性流感 疫苗的毒株选择。

papers.title: LucaCell: a sequence-centric foundation model for cross-species single-cell analysis
papers.abstract: Abstract Single-cell foundation models have transformed transcriptomic analysis, yet most rely on fixed gene identifiers that limit transfer across species and data types. Here we present LucaCell, a sequence-centric foundation model that represents genes through pre-trained mRNA sequence embeddings rather than static gene annotations. Gene expression is discretized into bins and modeled with a Transformer encoder, enabling sequence-informed cell representations that generalize across species and data types. Pre-training on 85 million human and mouse single cells, LucaCell enables cross-species and cross-modal cell type transfer in human, mouse, and lemur kidney datasets; alignment-free microbial embedding that distinguishes more than 50 bacterial species while preserving intra-species physiological states; and accurate host-virus interaction prediction across five influenza A virus strains. In addition, LucaCell incorporates donor-specific exonic SNPs to refine gene expression reconstruction and improves perturbation response prediction. Together, these results show that transcript-sequence information provides a transferable prior for single-cell foundation modeling across species, modalities, and biological contexts.

Page 2/33 Abstract Single-cell foundation models have transformed transcriptomic analysis, yet most rely on fixed gene identifiers that limit transfer across species and data types. Here we present LucaCell, a sequence- centric foundation model that represents genes through pre-trained mRNA sequence embeddings rather than static gene annotations. Gene expression is discretized into bins and modeled with a Transformer encoder, enabling sequence-informed cell representations that generalize across species and data types. Pre-training on 85 million human and mouse single cells, LucaCell enables cross-species and cross-modal cell type transfer in human, mouse, and lemur kidney datasets; alignment-free microbial embedding that distinguishes more than 50 bacterial species while preserving intra-species physiological states; and accurate host-virus interaction prediction across five influenza A virus strains. In addition, LucaCell incorporates donor-specific exonic SNPs to refine gene expression reconstruction and improves perturbation response prediction. Together, these results show that transcript-sequence information provides a transferable prior for single-cell foundation modeling across species, modalities, and biological contexts. Introduction Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has transformed our ability to resolve the cellular composition and organization of complex biological systems. The rapid adoption of scRNA-seq has generated an expanding repository of data that now encompasses hundreds of millions of cells. Major international consortia and data initiatives, such as the Human Cell Atlas [1], the Tabula Sapiens [2], and the CZ CELLxGENE data portal [3], have consolidated this growing body of information and enabled systematic exploration of cellular states and regulatory programs. Deciphering gene expression networks within cells is essential for understanding fundamental biological processes, including cellular differentiation, organismal development, disease mechanisms, therapeutic responses, cellular reprogramming, and aging. Despite this potential, the high dimensionality, sparsity, and measurement noise of single-cell data, together with heterogeneity across samples, technologies, species, and data types, pose substantial challenges for traditional analytical frameworks. Current computational methods [4–6] still struggle to achieve unified integration of such large, multi-batch datasets, as they often rely on fixed mapping relationships that limit the transfer of information across batches, data types, and species. To address these challenges, the field has increasingly turned to foundation models, particularly large- scale neural networks pre-trained on large transcriptomic corpora. By leveraging Transformer-based architectures, foundation models such as Geneformer [7], scFoundation [8], scGPT [9], and CellFM [10] can capture contextual gene-gene relationships and learn latent cellular representations that generalize across experiments. Despite this progress, most existing foundation models treat genes as discrete symbols or identifiers, which limits their scalability to novel species, unannotated genes, and non- canonical genomic regions, thereby restricting their broader applicability in biological prediction. Moreover, while some recent cross-species models such as TranscriptFormer [11] and Universal Cell Embeddings (UCE) [12] have incorporated protein-sequence embeddings, they do not capture Page 3/33 untranslated regions (UTRs) that contribute to transcript-level regulation, and their reliance on amino acid sequences limits flexibility when modeling non-protein-coding contexts. To address these limitations, we introduce LucaCell, a nucleic acid sequence-centric foundation model for single-cell analysis. Departing from traditional identifier-based approaches, LucaCell represents genes through pre-trained mRNA sequence embeddings rather than relying solely on static gene annotations. This approach maps each gene into a high-dimensional latent space based on sequence information rather than discrete labels, enabling sequence-based representation across species and data types without requiring manual gene mapping. Unlike discrete identifiers that treat each gene as an independent symbol, sequence embeddings preserve information about sequence similarity and functional relatedness, allowing the model to recognize homologous genes even when names or annotations differ across species. By integrating these sequence-level biological priors into a Transformer-based architecture, LucaCell learns representations that reflect sequence-associated information and support scalable single-cell analysis across diverse settings. In this work, we show that LucaCell supports sequence-centric representation learning that reduces reliance on species-specific gene annotations and enables cross-species comparison without manual ortholog mapping. Pre-trained on 85 million human and mouse cells spanning 62 tissue origins and 18 disease conditions, LucaCell learns a scalable representation of cellular heterogeneity. The model also incorporates nucleotide-level sequence information that captures variation not reflected in protein-level aggregation and supports virtual cell applications, including in silico perturbation modeling and cell- pathogen interaction prediction. Together, these results suggest that transcript sequence information can improve the transferability of single-cell foundation models across species and biological contexts. Results Sequence-centric gene representation and pre-training of LucaCell Gene representation plays a central role in single-cell foundation models. We developed LucaCell, a sequence-centric foundation model that represents genes through their intrinsic mRNA sequences, thereby reducing dependence on predefined gene annotations (Fig. 1a). To operationalize this design, each gene is encoded by an mRNA sequence embedding derived from the LucaOne foundation model [13], and expression values are discretized into bins for model input. This sequence-centric tokenization supports transfer across species and data types without requiring a fixed gene-ID vocabulary, thereby distinguishing LucaCell from existing single-cell foundation models (Table S1). Using a Transformer- based encoder architecture, LucaCell learns contextual gene relationships through a masked gene modeling objective that predicts masked expression bins from local cellular context. To capture global cellular heterogeneity, LucaCell was successfully pre-trained on 85 million single cells, including 67 million human and 18 million mouse scRNA-seq profiles spanning 62 tissue origins and 18 pathological states (Fig. 1b, S1). This sequence-based framework enables LucaCell to be applied to Page 4/33 traditionally challenging downstream tasks, such as cross-species cell type annotation, alignment-free cell embedding, variant-associated gene expression modeling, and cell-virus interaction prediction (Fig. 1c). a, Schematic of the LucaCell tokenization and pre-training framework. Genes are represented by mRNA sequence embeddings derived from LucaOne and discretized expression bins. LucaCell is trained with a masked gene modeling objective to predict masked expression bins from cellular context using a Transformer encoder. b, Tissue and clinical composition of the 85-million-cell pre-training corpus. c, Sequence-informed downstream applications of LucaCell, including cross-species cell type annotation, alignment-free cell embedding, sequence-level perturbation prediction and host-virus interaction modeling. Sequence-centric representations enable cross-species and cross- modal cell type transfer Accurately transferring cell type annotations across species and modalities remains a fundamental challenge, as it requires models to capture conserved regulatory programs despite species- and modality-specific variation. To assess whether sequence-derived gene representations improve transferability, we designed a transfer learning framework across four kidney datasets annotated with 11 shared cell types: human scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq [14], gray mouse lemur (Microcebus murinus) scRNA-seq [15], and mouse scRNA-seq [16], with the mouse scRNA-seq held out as a completely unseen test set (Fig. 2a). LucaCell yielded strong performance on seen species, achieving a test accuracy (ACC) of 0.937 (macro F1 = 0.921) for human scRNA-seq and 0.961 (macro F1 = 0.908) for lemur scRNA- seq. For the more challenging chromatin accessibility modality (human scATAC-seq), the model achieved a test accuracy of 0.653 (macro F1 = 0.516). On the completely unseen mouse dataset, LucaCell maintained moderate generalization performance (accuracy = 0.650, macro F1 = 0.493), indicating that sequence-informed representations support transfer across species. To investigate the structure of these representations across modalities and species, we projected cell embeddings from the pooling layer (the representation vectors) using UMAP. The projection showed that human scATAC-seq cells formed a distinct cluster separated from RNA-based modalities, while retaining cell type-specific structure (Fig. 2b, S2). When granular subtypes were aggregated into five major cell types, classification accuracy on human scATAC-seq data increased to 0.877 (macro F1 = 0.791; Fig. 2c), suggesting that LucaCell captures conserved cellular identity signals despite modality-specific noise. However, performance was lower for scATAC-seq subtype identification than for transcriptomic tasks, likely reflecting the sparsity and high dimensionality of chromatin accessibility data. Page 5/33 UMAP visualization and Euclidean distance analysis showed that human and mouse scRNA-seq embeddings were more tightly integrated than human and lemur embeddings in this kidney-specific context (Fig. 2b, d). This pattern is notable given the closer phylogenetic relationship between humans and lemurs. To examine this pattern, we compared the transcriptional conservation and sequence similarity of orthologous genes across three species. Marker-gene analysis showed that human and mouse shared a larger set of orthologous markers across most cell types than either species did with lemur, indicating stronger conservation of renal transcriptional programs between human and mouse (Fig. 2e, S3). In contrast, pairwise comparisons of sequence embeddings for 13 highly conserved orthologous markers shared by all three species showed no significant differences in sequence-level distances among species pairs (Fig. 2f). Notably, when mouse gene sequences were randomly replaced with sequences from other mouse genes while keeping the downstream model architecture and expression bins unchanged, prediction performance dropped sharply (accuracy = 0.25, macro F1 = 0.05), indicating that intact sequence-derived embeddings are important for cross-species transfer. Together, these results indicate that sequence-derived gene representations provide a foundation for cross- species transfer. The extent to which cells align to the same cell type across species, however, is still governed by the conservation of gene expression programs. a, Schematic of the sequence-aware transfer learning framework. Sequence-centric cell representations are processed through an MLP classifier to predict cell type identities across species and modalities. b, UMAP projection of LucaCell-derived cell embeddings, colored by species and modality. c, Confusion matrix showing cross-modal cell type prediction across five major cell types in human scATAC-seq data. d, Heatmap of mean pairwise Euclidean distances between cell embeddings across the species and modalities. e, Venn diagram showing the overlap of marker genes identified across all cell types in human, mouse and lemur. f, Pairwise distances between orthologous marker-gene sequence embeddings across species pairs. Statistical significance was assessed using a paired t-test; n.s., not significant (P > 0.05). Sequence-informed embeddings extend to alignment-free and read- level microbial representation To further examine whether this sequence-centric representation generalizes beyond canonical single- cell transcriptomic inputs, we next applied LucaCell to alignment-free and read-level cell representation. Single-microbe RNA sequencing (smRNA-seq) offers the potential to capture functional and physiological heterogeneity at the level of individual microbes[17–19], but applying current single-cell foundation models to these data still typically requires complex genome-alignment and reference-based Page 6/33 preprocessing pipelines. To address these limitations, we trained a downstream classifier with LucaCell embeddings derived from raw RNA-sequencing reads and fixed expression bins to predict microbial taxonomic and functional states without genome alignment (Fig. 3a). For taxonomic classification, we trained the downstream model on a 54-class task curated from a human gut smRNA-seq dataset [20], comprising the 53 most prevalent species and an ‘unidentifiable’ category. The model achieved a test accuracy of 84.1% (macro F1 score = 0.78). To compare with a purely sequence-based model, we stacked LucaOne sequence embeddings from the same sequencing reads for taxonomic classification, which achieved 82.1% test accuracy (macro F1 score = 0.76), suggesting that the fixed expression bin may serve as a contextual placeholder that improves the aggregation of sequence embeddings into a more informative cell-level representation. Unsupervised clustering of LucaCell embeddings from held- out microbes separated different species into distinct clusters (Fig. 3b). In addition, some species, such as Neobittarella massiliensis and MGYG000004894, formed multiple subclusters, suggesting that the model may capture intra-species heterogeneity. To examine whether these raw-read embeddings reflect physiologically relevant transitions, we applied the trained model to an independent bacterial culture smRNA-seq dataset [21] comprising four species: Acinetobacter baumannii (Aba), Escherichia coli (Eco), Klebsiella pneumoniae (Kpn), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pae). The dataset included Eco cells exposed to ciprofloxacin for 0, 1, 2, and 4 hours, as well as two species (Pae and Kpn) that were not among the 53 labelled species in the training cohort, providing a test on unlabelled taxa. Clustering of the learned embeddings separated both labelled and unlabelled species and also resolved longitudinal treatment dynamics (Fig. 3c). For Eco, the embeddings distinguished untreated cells (0 hours) from antibiotic-stressed cells (1, 2, and 4 hours), indicating that LucaCell can separate microbial physiological states associated with drug exposure. Furthermore, the subclusters identified by LucaCell’s alignment-free embeddings for Pae were concordant with those derived from traditional alignment-based gene expression matrices (Fig. 3d, e), as quantified by an Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) of 0.864 and a normalized mutual information (NMI) of 0.785, suggesting that raw-read latent representations can recover biologically meaningful structure comparable to gene-expression-based analyses. Moreover, LucaCell’s alignment-free embeddings achieved higher Silhouette and Calinski-Harabasz scores, and a lower Davies-Bouldin score than gene expression matrices, indicating improved cluster compactness and separation relative to alignment- based expression matrices. Differentially expressed gene (DEG) analysis showed that Pae cluster 0 was enriched for stress-response genes, including katA, azu, and arcD, whereas cluster 1 was dominated by translational machinery and denitrification genes (Fig. 3f). This pattern suggests the coexistence of physiologically distinct subpopulations within a single culture. Taken together, these results indicate that LucaCell provides an alignment-free framework that can both distinguish microbial species and resolve transcriptionally distinct physiological states within species. a, Schematic of the alignment-free microbial representation framework. Instead of aligned gene-count matrices, LucaCell processes raw sequencing reads directly. For each single-microbe, up to 8,192 reads Page 7/33 are randomly subsampled, with their expression bins uniformly set to 50 to encode read presence (Methods). b, UMAP projection of LucaCell embeddings from human gut microbial smRNA-seq data. c, UMAP visualization of raw-read embeddings from an independent validation cohort containing unseen species, resolving taxonomic identities and drug-induced physiological transitions within Eco subpopulations. d, UMAP projection of the Pae gene expression matrix, colored by alignment-free clusters identified in c. e, The same UMAP projection as in d, colored by clusters derived from gene expression matrix, showing agreement between read-based and expression-based embeddings. f, Volcano plot of DEGs between Pae clusters 0 (blue) and 1 (orange), as shown in e. The top 20 DEGs with the lowest adjusted P-values are labeled. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the limitations of existing single-cell foundation models that rely on fixed gene identifiers, which hinder cross-species and cross-modal analysis. The background highlights the need for more flexible and transferable models in transcriptomic studies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study presents LucaCell, a sequence-centric foundation model, and demonstrates its application across human, mouse, and lemur kidney datasets. It also evaluates its performance in distinguishing bacterial species and predicting host-virus interactions.
analysis.methods: LucaCell uses pre-trained mRNA sequence embeddings to represent genes, discretizes gene expression into bins, and models them with a Transformer encoder. It incorporates donor-specific exonic SNPs to refine gene expression reconstruction and improve perturbation response prediction.
analysis.main_results: LucaCell enables cross-species and cross-modal cell type transfer in human, mouse, and lemur kidney datasets. It distinguishes more than 50 bacterial species while preserving intra-species physiological states and accurately predicts host-virus interactions across five influenza A virus strains.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that transcript-sequence information provides a transferable prior for single-cell foundation modeling, offering a novel approach that generalizes across species, modalities, and biological contexts.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings have implications for improving cross-species and cross-modal analysis in transcriptomics, which can enhance understanding of host-virus interactions and support more accurate surveillance and diagnosis of influenza viruses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to abstract-only evidence, which may restrict the depth of analysis. However, the results are supported by pre-training on large datasets and demonstrate strong generalization capabilities across species and data types.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces LucaCell, a sequence-centric foundation model designed to overcome the limitations of traditional single-cell transcriptomic analysis by using pre-trained mRNA sequence embeddings instead of fixed gene identifiers. The model is tested across human, mouse, and lemur kidney datasets, demonstrating its ability to generalize across species and data types. It also accurately predicts host-virus interactions across five influenza A virus strains and distinguishes over 50 bacterial species. papers.title_zh: LucaCell:一种以序列为中心的基础模型,用于跨物种单细胞分析
papers.source_body_en: Abstract Single-cell foundation models have transformed transcriptomic analysis, yet most rely on fixed gene identifiers that limit transfer across species and data types. Here we present LucaCell, a sequence-centric foundation model that represents genes through pre-trained mRNA sequence embeddings rather than static gene annotations. Gene expression is discretized into bins and modeled with a Transformer encoder, enabling sequence-informed cell representations that generalize across species and data types. Pre-training on 85 million human and mouse single cells, LucaCell enables cross-species and cross-modal cell type transfer in human, mouse, and lemur kidney datasets; alignment-free microbial embedding that distinguishes more than 50 bacterial species while preserving intra-species physiological states; and accurate host-virus interaction prediction across five influenza A virus strains. In addition, LucaCell incorporates donor-specific exonic SNPs to refine gene expression reconstruction and improves perturbation response prediction. Together, these results show that transcript-sequence information provides a transferable prior for single-cell foundation modeling across species, modalities, and biological contexts.

papers.title: Förster Resonance Energy Transfer-Based Selective Detection of Influenza Viruses Using N-Doped Sialic Acid Carbon Dots.
papers.abstract: We report the rational design and synthesis of nitrogen-doped sialic acid-derived carbon dots (SiaMPDA CDs) with excitation-independent green emission and high quantum yield and demonstrate their application as efficient Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) donors for the selective detection of influenza A virus (IAV) subtypes. The surface functionalization of the CDs with sialic acid moieties enables specific molecular recognition of the viral hemagglutinin (HA) protein via multivalent hydrogen-bonding interactions. In combination with Rhodamine B (RhB) as an acceptor, the SiaMPDA-RhB pair exhibits efficient FRET under native conditions. Upon interaction with IAV (H3N2 and H1N1), the FRET system displays anomalous spectral behavior characterized by a simultaneous increase in both donor and acceptor emission intensities without any spectral shift. Mechanistic investigations suggest the formation of a ternary IAV-SiaMPDA-RhB complex, wherein long-range charge transfer coupled with FRET governs the observed fluorescence response. Control experiments with proteins, membrane vesicles, and liposomes confirm that the signal specificity arises from targeted interactions between the sialic acid functionalities of the CDs and the viral surface proteins. The sensing platform enables selective and sensitive detection of IAV subtypes in the picomolar range, comparable to existing carbon dot-based detection systems. These findings establish N-doped sialic acid carbon dots as promising nanoscale probes for virus detection and provide insights into charge-transfer-coupled FRET mechanisms in complex bionano interfaces.

source_records.abstract: We report the rational design and synthesis of nitrogen-doped sialic acid-derived carbon dots (SiaMPDA CDs) with excitation-independent green emission and high quantum yield and demonstrate their application as efficient Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) donors for the selective detection of influenza A virus (IAV) subtypes. The surface functionalization of the CDs with sialic acid moieties enables specific molecular recognition of the viral hemagglutinin (HA) protein via multivalent hydrogen-bonding interactions. In combination with Rhodamine B (RhB) as an acceptor, the SiaMPDA-RhB pair exhibits efficient FRET under native conditions. Upon interaction with IAV (H3N2 and H1N1), the FRET system displays anomalous spectral behavior characterized by a simultaneous increase in both donor and acceptor emission intensities without any spectral shift. Mechanistic investigations suggest the formation of a ternary IAV-SiaMPDA-RhB complex, wherein long-range charge transfer coupled with FRET governs the observed fluorescence response. Control experiments with proteins, membrane vesicles, and liposomes confirm that the signal specificity arises from targeted interactions between the sialic acid functionalities of the CDs and the viral surface proteins. The sensing platform enables selective and sensitive detection of IAV subtypes in the picomolar range, comparable to existing carbon dot-based detection systems. These findings establish N-doped sialic acid carbon dots as promising nanoscale probes for virus detection and provide insights into charge-transfer-coupled FRET mechanisms in complex bionano interfaces.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在开发一种新型方法用于流感A病毒亚型的选择性检测,以应对对季节性流感病毒更高效和特异性诊断工具的需求。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究涉及在受控实验条件下设计、合成和应用氮掺杂唾液酸衍生碳点(SiaMPDA CDs)作为FRET供体,用于检测流感A病毒亚型,特别是H3N2和H1N1。
elements_zh.methods: 研究人员合成了SiaMPDA CDs,并在其表面引入唾液酸基团,以通过多价氢键相互作用实现对病毒血凝素(HA)蛋白的特异性分子识别。他们将这些碳点与罗丹明B(RhB)结合作为受体,构建了一个FRET系统。
elements_zh.main_results: 当与IAV亚型H3N2和H1N1相互作用时,FRET系统表现出异常的光谱行为,特征是供体和受体发射强度同时增加,而没有光谱位移。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 所观察到的荧光响应归因于三元IAV-SiaMPDA-RhB复合物的形成,其中长程电荷转移与FRET共同调控其行为,为理解生物纳米界面机制提供了新的视角。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为流感A亚型的选择性与灵敏检测提供了有前景的平台,可能增强监测和季节性流感病毒的诊断能力。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究仅限于摘要层面的报告,其证据基于受控实验,而没有临床或现场验证,因此对研究结果在现实场景中的适用性信心中等。

papers.abstract_zh: 我们报告了氮掺杂唾液酸衍生碳点(SiaMPDA CDs)的合理设计与合成,这些碳点具有与激发波长无关的绿色发射和高量子产率,并展示了其作为高效福斯特共振能量转移(FRET)供体用于流感A病毒(IAV)亚型选择性检测的应用。通过在碳点表面引入唾液酸基团,使其能够通过多价氢键相互作用特异性识别病毒血凝素(HA)蛋白。在与罗丹明B(RhB)作为受体结合后,SiaMPDA-RhB对在天然条件下表现出高效的FRET。当与IAV(H3N2和H1N1)相互作用时,FRET系统表现出异常的光谱行为,特征是供体和受体发射强度同时增加,而没有光谱位移。机制研究提示形成了一个三元IAV-SiaMPDA-RhB复合物,其中长程电荷转移与FRET共同调控所观察到的荧光响应。与蛋白质、膜囊泡和脂质体进行的对照实验确认,信号特异性来源于碳点唾液酸功能团与病毒表面蛋白之间的靶向相互作用。该传感平台能够选择性且灵敏地检测IAV亚型,在皮摩尔范围内,其性能与现有的碳点基检测系统相当。这些发现确立了氮掺杂唾液酸碳点作为病毒检测的有前景的纳米探针,并提供了对复杂生物纳米界面中电荷转移耦合FRET机制的见解。

This study found that while 67% of HCWs received the influenza vaccine and 84% received at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine, concerns about vaccine safety, particularly for COVID-19, highlight the need for targeted interventions to improve vaccine acceptance and coverage. Abstract Introduction Respiratory viruses like influenza and SARS-CoV-2 pose ongoing global health threats, especially within healthcare settings where healthcare workers (HCWs) face elevated risks of exposure. By late 2023, COVID-19 was transitioning from a pandemic to an endemic phase globally and within Côte d’Ivoire, with sustained transmission but reduced severity due to accumulated immunity and vaccination coverage. Despite the World Health Organization’s recommendation to prioritize HCWs for seasonal influenza vaccination, achieving optimal coverage remains a challenge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) such as Côte d’Ivoire.COVID-19 vaccines were introduced in Côte d’Ivoire in early 2021, with healthcare workers prioritized during the initial phases of the national vaccination campaign, followed by gradual expansion to the general population. This study aimed to assess the knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding influenza and COVID-19 vaccination among healthcare workers in Côte d’Ivoire. Method This cross-sectional survey was conducted in November 2023 across two urban regions of Côte d’IvoireCôte d’Ivoire to assess HCWs’ knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding influenza and COVID-19 vaccination. A total of 1,454 HCWs were interviewed. Descriptive statistics, logistic regression, and chi-square tests were used for analysis. Results Findings revealed that 78% of HCWs perceived influenza as potentially leading to severe illness or death, while 95% held this view for COVID-19. Although 79% considered the influenza vaccine safe, only 58% felt the same about the COVID-19 vaccine. In terms of uptake, 67% had received the influenza vaccine in the most recent season, and 84% had received at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose. HCWs who had received an influenza vaccine before the COVID-19 pandemic were significantly more likely to have received both the most recent influenza vaccine and at least one dose of the COVID-19 vaccine (p < 0.001). Older HCWs also demonstrated higher vaccine uptake than their younger counterparts (p < 0.001). Conclusion These results underscore the importance of leveraging existing influenza vaccination infrastructure to support broader vaccine acceptance strategies. Improving HCW vaccine coverage can strengthen health system resilience and support pandemic preparedness in the Côte d’Ivoire and similar settings. 1 Introduction Infectious diseases such as influenza and COVID-19 continue to pose significant threats to global public health, particularly within healthcare settings where healthcare workers are at heightened risk of exposure [1, 2]. Vaccination against these diseases is widely acknowledged as a fundamental preventive measure to safeguard both healthcare workers and the patients they serve, and the World Health Organization (WHO) Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) has recommended healthcare workers as a prioritised risk group for seasonal influenza vaccination [3]. A key challenge in public health is ensuring optimal vaccination coverage among healthcare workers (HCWs), particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) such as Côte d’Ivoire. This difficulty is well documented in academic literature and public health reports. For example, studies on the COVID-19 vaccine rollout in LMICs show that despite HCWs being a priority group, vaccination rates often remained low for extended periods due to logistical hurdles, vaccine hesitancy, and supply chain issues. Data from Côte d’Ivoire and other countries in the African region consistently demonstrate that achieving high vaccination coverage was a significant and ongoing struggle months after the vaccine was introduced. This reality highlights the complex and multifaceted challenges of vaccine implementation beyond just initial availability [4]. Influenza is a viral respiratory illness that can lead to severe complications and even death, particularly among vulnerable populations. Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for healthcare workers to mitigate the risk of transmission within healthcare settings and to protect both them and their patients [5]. Similarly, the emergence of the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, responsible for the COVID-19 pandemic, has underscored the urgent need for vaccination to control the spread of the virus and prevent severe illness and death. Despite the clear benefits of vaccination, healthcare workers in LMICs often face barriers to vaccination, including limited access to vaccines, vaccine hesitancy, and misinformation about vaccine safety and efficacy [6]. These challenges are further compounded by socio-economic factors, healthcare infrastructure limitations, and competing public health priorities, which is especially true for influenza vaccination. A program to provide influenza vaccination to healthcare workers began in 2011 through a partnership with the Partnership for Influenza Vaccine Introduction (PIVI) [7]. In Cote d’Ivoire, COVID-19 vaccines first became available through the COVAX Facility in February 2021, with the national vaccination campaign launched in March 2021 prioritising healthcare and other frontline workers as an at-risk group, followed by phased mass vaccination campaigns from December 2021 that progressively expanded eligibility to the general population. As in many LMICs, this rollout depended heavily on programmatic access, including vaccine supply through COVAX, cold-chain logistics, and community mobilisation, and national implementation strategies shaped how quickly and completely HCWs achieved coverage. Because our survey was conducted in November 2023, well beyond this initial rollout period, respondents’ risk perceptions, vaccination behaviours, and acceptance patterns likely reflect a more settled, post-peak phase of the pandemic rather than the urgency of the initial emergency rollout. Recent evidence suggests that countries with established influenza vaccination programs have demonstrated a better ability to distribute and administer COVID-19 vaccines efficiently. The infrastructure and mechanisms developed for seasonal influenza vaccination campaigns, including vaccine procurement, distribution networks, and vaccination sites, have provided a foundation for the rollout of COVID-19 vaccination programs [8]. Moreover, healthcare workers involved in influenza vaccination campaigns often possess the necessary skills and experience to implement COVID-19 vaccination initiatives effectively [9]. Leveraging existing influenza vaccination programs can therefore serve as a strategic approach to enhance COVID-19 vaccination efforts, particularly in LMICs where healthcare infrastructure may be limited [10]. Understanding the interplay between influenza and COVID-19 vaccination programs and their potential synergies is crucial for optimising vaccination strategies and maximising public health impact in countries like Côte d’Ivoire. Understanding the knowledge, attitudes, and practices surrounding influenza and COVID-19 vaccination among healthcare workers in the Côte d’Ivoire is essential for informing targeted interventions to improve vaccine acceptance and coverage. This study aimed to assess the knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding influenza and COVID-19 vaccination among healthcare workers in Côte d’Ivoire and to identify factors associated with vaccine uptake. 2 Methods 2.1 Sample size determination/sampling method Survey sites and facility-level target enrolment were selected using a probability proportional to size (PPS) approach, based on a comprehensive list of all hospitals and primary healthcare clinics (PHCs) and their total number of staff. This ensured that facilities with larger healthcare worker (HCW) populations had a higher probability of selection. The study population included a range of healthcare worker cadres with direct patient contact, including doctors, nurses, midwives, pharmacists, caregivers, and other allied health professionals. A cluster sampling design was employed, where each selected health facility constituted a cluster. Within each cluster, HCWs were recruited proportionally based on facility size, with an average of approximately 30 participants per facility. Participants within clusters were approached consecutively until the allocated sample size per facility was achieved. The sample size (n) was calculated using the formula for finite populations with no a priori hypothesis testing between groups (i.e., vaccinated vs. unvaccinated individuals) [11]: n = N / [1 + N(e)2], where N represents the total target population and e is the desired precision level (0.05). To account for the cluster-based sampling design, a design effect (DE) of 4.75 was applied, calculated as: DE = 1 + mα2μ, where m is the average cluster size (30 participants), α is the intra-cluster correlation coefficient (0.5), and μ is the expected outcome prevalence (0.5). The sample size was further adjusted for an anticipated non-response rate of 20% using the formula: ns = n / (1 − r). Based on these assumptions and standard sample size tables for cluster surveys, the required sample size ranged from 1,346 to 2,199 participants. However, considering operational feasibility and the defined sampling frame, a final sample of 1,454 healthcare workers was included in the study. 2.2 Survey method This cross-sectional survey was conducted in November 2023. The survey included questions for health workers’ understanding of influenza and COVID-19 diseases, their knowledge of vaccines, and their willingness to be vaccinated. The study also explored health workers’ active recommendation practices for vaccines. By following components of the Health Belief Model, we aimed to identify factors influencing vaccine acceptance among healthcare professionals in Côte d’Ivoire [12]. Health workers play a critical role in promoting public health and preventing infectious diseases. Understanding their perspectives on vaccination is essential for effective vaccine implementation. The inclusion criteria for this study were healthcare workers in Côte d’Ivoire aged 18 years and above, with direct patient contact, who provided informed consent to participate. Healthcare workers without direct patient contact, those below 18 years of age, or those who declined consent were excluded. The survey assessed key domains of knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) related to influenza and COVID-19 vaccination using a structured questionnaire. Knowledge was evaluated through questions on disease severity, transmission, and vaccine effectiveness, while attitudes were assessed using Likert-scale responses (e.g., strongly agree to strongly disagree) on perceptions of vaccine safety and effectiveness. Practices were measured through self-reported vaccination status, willingness to be vaccinated, and vaccine recommendation behaviors. Responses were categorised and analysed to generate composite indicators for each KAP domain, guided by constructs from the Health Belief Model. Côte d’IvoireTrained data collectors/research assistants participantsapproached potential participants, explaining the study’s goals and objectives, and invited health workers who met the inclusion criteria to participate. Informed consent was obtained from all participants. The questionnaire assessed their understanding of both diseases, vaccine-related knowledge, and their personal vaccination preferences. For this study, COVID-19 vaccination status was defined as receipt of at least one dose of any WHO-authorised COVID-19 vaccine. We adopted this pragmatic single-dose threshold, rather than requiring a completed primary series, because the number of doses constituting a full primary series varies by vaccine platform in our setting (for example, two doses for most mRNA and viral-vector vaccines, compared with a single dose for the Janssen/Johnson & Johnson vaccine); a single-dose definition therefore provided the most consistent measure of any vaccination exposure across the heterogeneous vaccine platforms received by participants. We acknowledge that this approach may limit direct comparability with studies that define vaccination status based on a completed primary series or booster dose, and we address this further as a limitation. 2.3 Data analysis The statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS software, version 28, the latest iteration at the time of this study [13]. The initial phase of the analysis involved a descriptive examination of the demographic and socioeconomic characteristics of the study participants. This included the computation of frequencies, means, standard deviations, and other relevant summary statistics to provide an overview of the participant pool. Subsequently, the relationship between each covariate and the outcome variables was assessed. Binary logistic regression was employed to evaluate the strength and direction of these associations, quantified by the regression coefficients. Additionally, the Chi-Square Cross-Tabulation analysis was utilised to examine the associations between categorical variables. To account for potential confounding factors, variables that demonstrated an association with the outcome variable at a significance level of approximately 20% were included in the multivariable logistic regression analysis. This approach allowed for the adjustment of odds ratios (AOR) to control for these confounders, thereby isolating the effect of the primary independent variables on the outcome. The results of the final model were presented as adjusted odds ratios (AOR) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CI). Statistical significance was determined using a p-value threshold of less than 0.05. This threshold indicates that there is less than a 5% probability that the observed associations are due to random chance, thus providing a measure of the reliability of the results. 3 Result From the KAP survey (as shown in Table 1), among healthcare workers, the majority of participants, 70.5%, were female, with the largest age group being 35–39 years old, accounting for 32%. Most workers had 5–9 years of experience in healthcare. Regarding COVID-19 vaccination, 84.38% of rural and 83.47% of urban healthcare workers were vaccinated. During the pandemic, 87.44% recommended COVID-19 vaccines, and 78.64% were in favour of annual vaccination. In terms of treating complications, 13.41% had dealt with life-threatening complications from influenza, and 5.79% from COVID-19, highlighting the impact of these diseases on patient health and the importance of vaccination. Multivariable analysis showed that prior influenza vaccination was strongly associated with COVID-19 vaccination uptake (p < 0.001). Age was also significantly associated with vaccination status (p < 0.001). However, gender, years of experience, and professional cadre were not significantly associated with COVID-19 vaccination uptake (p > 0.05). The primary outcome variable for the multivariable analysis was COVID-19 vaccination uptake, defined as receipt of at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine (Yes/No). Independent variables considered included age, sex, professional cadre, years of healthcare service, prior influenza vaccination history, recommendation of COVID-19 vaccines during the pandemic, and experience managing patients hospitalized with influenza or COVID-19 complications. There was a significant portion of health workers (as shown in Table 2) who recognized the severity of influenza for high-risk groups. Over 50% in most groups agree or strongly agree that it can lead to serious outcomes. The belief in the effectiveness of the influenza vaccine is even higher, with over 70% of health workers and the general population strongly agreeing that vaccination can reduce severe illness. Safety perceptions of the vaccine are also positive, with a majority considering it safe across all groups. This statistic underscores the critical consensus on the impact of influenza, the protective value of vaccination, and its perceived safety among diverse groups. Most respondents (as seen on Table 3) agreed or strongly agreed that COVID-19 could cause severe illness or death among high-risk groups, including the elderly (96%), persons with chronic conditions (95%), pregnant women (94%), and immunocompromised individuals (95%). However, fewer HCWs (89%) perceived children under 5 as being at similar risk. In terms of vaccine safety, perceptions were generally moderate, with only 57% of respondents viewing COVID-19 vaccines as “safe” or “very safe” for health workers themselves, and slightly lower perceived safety for vulnerable groups such as pregnant women (57%) and immunocompromised persons (57%). Regarding vaccine effectiveness, over two-thirds of HCWs (67–70%) strongly agreed that COVID-19 vaccines significantly reduce the risk of severe illness across all groups, particularly for the general population (70%) and for themselves (70%). Healthcare workers demonstrated high knowledge of the severity of both influenza and COVID-19. For influenza, most respondents agreed or strongly agreed that the disease could lead to severe illness, hospitalization, or death across multiple population groups (Table 2). Similarly, over 90% of respondents recognized that COVID-19 could cause serious illness or death among high-risk groups (Table 3). Knowledge of vaccine effectiveness was also high. papers.title: Co-infection models of Staphylococcus aureus and respiratory viruses reveal synergistic interactions counteracted by a bithiazole derivative
papers.abstract: Viral-bacterial co-infections represent a major contributor to global morbidity and mortality. In influenza virus infections, secondary bacterial pneumonia occurs in approximately 20–30% of cases and is associated with an increased risk of shock, mechanical ventilation, and even mortality. Bacterial superinfections are frequent causes of mortality in influenza severe infections and have been a major cause of morbidity and mortality also in COVID-19 patients. Staphylococcus aureus has been identified as one of the most prevalent bacterial pathogens among hospitalized and non-hospitalized patients who have tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 or influenza virus infections. Generally, antibiotic therapy is administered to at-risk patients to preclude bacterial over-infections by eliminating susceptible pathogens, increasing selective pressure favoring antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Due to the recognized public health problem of antibiotic resistance, the exploration of alternative therapies to counteract or prevent the development of serious virus/bacteria co-infections has become a critical research priority. The present study aimed to investigate the interactions between coronavirus or influenza A virus, and S. aureus in a co-infection model and to investigate the ability of a known antiviral/antibacterial compound, the bithiazole derivative MR335, to counteract the interaction between the two pathogens. The co-infection models were established using the pulmonary cell line A549 and the bronchial cell line BEAS-2B. The synergistic interaction between virus and bacteria were assessed through standard viral titration assays and bacterial adhesion and invasion assays. The bithiazole compound, MR335, showed both antiviral and antibacterial activity at distinct concentrations. In particular, it effectively counteracted the synergistic interactions between respiratory viruses and S. aureus at concentration that retained antiviral but not antibacterial activity. Notably, eradication of viruses impaired bacterial invasion, suggesting their synergistic cooperation and opening the way to alternative therapies that prevent bacterial superinfection without resorting to conventional antibiotics.

In influenza virus infections, secondary bacterial pneumonia occurs in approximately 20–30% of cases and is associated with an increased risk of shock, mechanical ventilation, and even mortality. Bacterial superinfections are frequent causes of mortality in influenza severe infections and have been a major cause of morbidity and mortality also in COVID-19 patients. Staphylococcus aureus has been identified as one of the most prevalent bacterial pathogens among hospitalized and non-hospitalized patients who have tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 or influenza virus infections. Generally, antibiotic therapy is administered to at-risk patients to preclude bacterial over-infections by eliminating susceptible pathogens, increasing selective pressure favoring antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Due to the recognized public health problem of antibiotic resistance, the exploration of alternative therapies to counteract or prevent the development of serious virus/bacteria co-infections has become a critical research priority. The present study aimed to investigate the interactions between coronavirus or influenza A virus, and S. aureus in a co-infection model and to investigate the ability of a known antiviral/antibacterial compound, the bithiazole derivative MR335, to counteract the interaction between the two pathogens. The co-infection models were established using the pulmonary cell line A549 and the bronchial cell line BEAS-2B. The synergistic interaction between virus and bacteria were assessed through standard viral titration assays and bacterial adhesion and invasion assays. The bithiazole compound, MR335, showed both antiviral and antibacterial activity at distinct concentrations. In particular, it effectively counteracted the synergistic interactions between respiratory viruses and S. aureus at concentration that retained antiviral but not antibacterial activity. Notably, eradication of viruses impaired bacterial invasion, suggesting their synergistic cooperation and opening the way to alternative therapies that prevent bacterial superinfection without resorting to conventional antibiotics.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 病毒-细菌共感染是全球发病率和死亡率的重要因素。预防细菌过度感染的抗生素治疗会增加选择压力,促进抗生素耐药细菌的生长,凸显了寻找替代疗法的必要性。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究旨在通过肺和支气管细胞系建立共感染模型,研究冠状病毒或流感A病毒与金黄色葡萄球菌之间的相互作用,并评估二噻唑衍生物MR335对抗这些相互作用的能力。
elements_zh.methods: 通过标准病毒滴度测定和细菌黏附与侵入实验评估病毒与细菌之间的协同作用。二噻唑化合物MR335在不同浓度下表现出抗病毒活性和抗菌活性。
elements_zh.main_results: 二噻唑化合物MR335在保留抗病毒活性但不具有抗菌活性的浓度下,有效抵消了呼吸道病毒与金黄色葡萄球菌之间的协同作用。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 本研究证明MR335能够抵消呼吸道病毒与金黄色葡萄球菌之间的协同作用,表明其可能作为替代疗法,用于预防细菌继发感染,而无需依赖传统抗生素。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可能有助于开发新的疗法,以预防严重的病毒/细菌共感染,从而应对抗生素耐药性的公共卫生问题。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 由于研究设计的局限性,包括使用细胞系,可能会影响结果的普遍适用性。由于证据仅基于摘要,其证据强度中等。

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the one-year mortality rate among adults hospitalized with seasonal influenza viruses in Southern Sweden, addressing the public health concern of understanding long-term outcomes following severe influenza infection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This was a retrospective observational study conducted in Southern Sweden between 2010 and 2020, focusing on adults hospitalized with influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), or B viruses.
analysis.methods: The study analyzed medical records of adults admitted to intensive care units with confirmed influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), or B infections, using a retrospective observational approach to evaluate one-year mortality rates.
analysis.main_results: The study reported a high one-year mortality rate of 30% among adults with influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), or B viruses who required intensive care.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the high mortality rate as indicative of the severity of influenza infections in adults requiring intensive care, highlighting the need for improved surveillance and management strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings underscore the importance of monitoring long-term outcomes in patients with severe seasonal influenza, informing future research and public health interventions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential biases in data collection, but the evidence is strong due to the clear focus on the target influenza viruses and the use of medical records from a well-defined region.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective observational study investigated the one-year mortality rate among adults hospitalized with seasonal influenza viruses in Southern Sweden. The study focused on influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B viruses, reporting a high mortality rate of 30% among those requiring intensive care. The authors interpreted these findings as highlighting the severity of influenza infections in this population, emphasizing the need for improved surveillance and management. The study's limitations include its retrospective nature and potential biases, but the evidence is considered strong due to the clear focus on the target viruses and the use of medical records from a defined region. The results have significant implications for understanding long-term outcomes in severe influenza cases and could inform future public health strategies.

elements_zh.main_results: 研究报告称,接受重症监护的感染流感甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09、甲型H3N2流感病毒或B病毒的成人患者中,一年内的死亡率发生率高达30%。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将高死亡率发生率解释为成人重症监护患者中流感感染严重性的指标,强调了改进监测和管理策略的必要性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现突显了对严重季节性流感患者进行长期结果监测的重要性,为未来的研究和公共卫生干预提供了依据。

(with photos) HKSAR Government strongly disapproves of and rejects annual report of European Commission CE and Principal Officials receive seasonal influenza vaccination (with photos) CE and Principal Officials receive seasonal influenza vaccination (with photos) ******************************************************************************** The Chief Executive, Mr John Lee, led a number of Principal Officials to receive seasonal influenza vaccination (SIV) today (September 23) and called on members of the public to get vaccinated as early as possible to build an immunity barrier in the community together and better protect their health and that of their family members. Mr Lee said, "Vaccination is one of the most effective means for preventing seasonal influenza and its complications, as well as reducing the risk of hospitalisation and death arising from influenza. I appeal to members of the public to get vaccinated as early as possible to protect themselves and their family members." Under the vigorous promotion by the Government, and with support from all sectors of the community, more than 2.03 million doses of vaccines were administered under various SIV programmes in the previous year (2025/26), with overall coverage rates of the target population remaining similar to those of the preceding year. Among children and adolescents, the SIV rate for persons aged 6 months to under 18 years reached 64.8 per cent, which is 13.1 percentage points higher than the average for the same period over the past three seasons (51.7 per cent). The vaccination rate for adolescents aged 12 to under 18 years reached 61.4 per cent, representing a substantial increase of 22.6 percentage points compared with the average for the same period over the past three seasons (38.8 per cent). The Government-subsidised SIV programmes, including the Vaccination Subsidy Scheme, the Government Vaccination Programme, the SIV School Outreach Programme and the Residential Care Home Vaccination Programme, provide free or subsidised influenza vaccinations to children and adolescents aged 6 months to under 18 years, adults aged 18 to 49 with chronic medical conditions (regardless of financial status), persons aged 50 or above (including the elderly living in residential care homes), pregnant women and healthcare workers, and others. To encourage and offer convenience to members of the public to receive SIV, the Government has implemented four optimising initiatives this year, namely optimising vaccine procurement arrangements with the diversified, non-single-supplier procurement approach; introducing a new Electronic Consent Form feature viaeHealth; increasing the number of influenza vaccine doses to 300 000 under the Pilot Scheme on Vaccine Procurement for Doctors and expanding the eligibility groups of doctors; as well as strengthening the mobilisation of community resources. The Government will also continue to implement the Civil Service Eligible Persons SIV Pilot Scheme this year. Since civil servants frequently interact with members of the public, vaccinations can not only better safeguard their health, but also help reduce the risk of influenza transmission in the community. The Secretary for Health, Professor Lo Chung-mau, said, "Various SIV programmes have been fully commenced on September 17 to provide free or subsidised SIV services for eligible persons. Since it takes about two weeks after receiving an SIV for antibodies to develop in the body and provide protection against influenza virus infection, I strongly urge members of the public to get vaccinated early." For more details, members of the public may call the Centre for Health Protection of the Department of Health at 2125 2125 or visit the Vaccination Schemes page. analysis.event: The Chief Executive, Mr John Lee, led Principal Officials in receiving seasonal influenza vaccination and urged the public to get vaccinated as early as possible to build an immunity barrier and protect health. The Government implemented SIV programmes and initiatives to promote vaccination.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: In the previous year (2025/26), more than 2.03 million doses were administered under various SIV programmes. Among children and adolescents, the SIV rate reached 64.8 per cent, a 13.1 percentage point increase compared to the average of the past three seasons. For adolescents aged 12 to under 18 years, the rate reached 61.4 per cent, a 22.6 percentage point increase compared to the past three seasons.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The Government has fully commenced SIV programmes on September 17, 2026, and implemented four optimising initiatives to encourage and offer convenience for vaccination. The vaccination rate for the target population is reported, and the Government continues to promote these programmes.

analysis.brief_en: On September 23, 2026, the Chief Executive of Hong Kong, Mr John Lee, led Principal Officials in receiving seasonal influenza vaccination, urging the public to get vaccinated early to build an immunity barrier and protect their health and that of their families. The Government has implemented various SIV programmes, including the Vaccination Subsidy Scheme, the Government Vaccination Programme, the SIV School Outreach Programme, and the Residential Care Home Vaccination Programme, to provide free or subsidised influenza vaccinations to eligible groups such as children and adolescents aged 6 months to under 18 years, adults with chronic medical conditions, persons aged 50 or above, pregnant women, and healthcare workers. In the previous year (2025/26), over 2.03 million doses were administered, with the SIV rate for children and adolescents reaching 64.8 per cent, a 13.1 percentage point increase compared to the average of the past three seasons. For adolescents aged 12 to under 18 years, the rate reached 61.4 per cent, a 22.6 percentage point increase. The Government has also introduced four optimising initiatives, including a new Electronic Consent Form and increased vaccine procurement, to enhance public access to SIV services. These efforts aim to reduce the risk of influenza transmission and hospitalisation, particularly among vulnerable groups.

For adolescents aged 12 to under 18 years, the rate reached 61.4 per cent, a 22.6 percentage point increase. The Government has also introduced four optimising initiatives, including a new Electronic Consent Form and increased vaccine procurement, to enhance public access to SIV services. Recommendations announced for influenza vaccine composition for the 2027 southern hemisphere influenza season 25 September 2026 News release Reading time: 2 min (537 words) العربية Español The World Health Organization (WHO) today announced its recommendations for the viral composition of influenza (or ‘flu’) vaccines for use in the 2027 southern hemisphere influenza season. The announcement was made following an international consultation on the composition of influenza virus vaccines. Seasonal influenza causes substantial illness and many hospitalizations each year. Regular updates to vaccine composition are needed because influenza viruses continually evolve. WHO’s recommendations are used by national vaccine regulatory agencies and pharmaceutical companies around the world to develop, produce, and license influenza vaccines for the following influenza season. This ensures that vaccines are closely matched to the viruses expected to circulate, offering the best possible protection against severe illness and death. Twice each year, WHO convenes experts from its Collaborating Centres and Essential Regulatory Laboratories to review surveillance data generated through the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) and other sources, and recommend vaccine compositions for upcoming influenza seasons. "For nearly 75 years, the WHO Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System has demonstrated the power of global solidarity in public health," said Dr Maria Van Kerhove, WHO's Director for Epidemic and Pandemic Management. "The commitment of countries and laboratories to share data, viruses and expertise enables WHO to make timely vaccine recommendations, strengthening our collective ability to detect and respond to emerging influenza threats. This is global public health collaboration at its best." From February to August 2026, influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2) and influenza B viruses circulated in varying proportions across all regions of the world, causing disease. Influenza A viruses were the most common in most regions, except Northern and Western Africa, North America and Eastern Asia, where influenza B viruses dominated. WHO recommends that vaccines for use in the 2027 southern hemisphere influenza season contain the following: Egg-based vaccines an A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus; an A/Darwin/1454/2025 (H3N2)-like virus; and a B/Tokyo/EIS13-175/2025 (B/Victoria lineage)-like virus. Cell culture-, recombinant protein- or nucleic acid-based vaccines an A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus; an A/Darwin/1415/2025 (H3N2)-like virus; and a B/Pennsylvania/14/2025 (B/Victoria lineage)-like virus. As part of the review, experts also looked at influenza viruses circulating in animals, particularly those that have caused infections in humans. These animal or zoonotic influenza viruses remain a significant concern because of their potential to cause pandemics. These biannual meetings include a detailed assessment of these viruses and the selection of new candidate vaccine viruses (CVVs) from contemporary zoonotic influenza viruses, which can be used rapidly to manufacture vaccines should a pandemic threat arise. Information on newly selected zoonotic influenza CVVs is available on the WHO website. About WHO Dedicated to the well-being of all people and guided by science, WHO leads and champions global efforts to give everyone, everywhere, an equal chance at a safe and healthy life. We are the United Nations’ agency for health that connects nations, partners and people in more than 150 locations – leading the world’s response to health emergencies, preventing disease, addressing the root causes of health issues and expanding access to medicines and health care. Our mission is to support all countries to promote, provide and protect health. “Together for health. Stand with science”, the theme of World Health Day 2026, marks a year-long campaign to highlight science as the foundation for protecting health and well-being worldwide. analysis.brief_en: The World Health Organization (WHO) announced on 25 September 2026 its recommendations for the 2027 southern hemisphere influenza vaccine composition. These recommendations were made following an international consultation involving experts from WHO's Collaborating Centres and Essential Regulatory Laboratories. The WHO Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) and other sources provided the surveillance data used to determine the vaccine strains. The focus of the recommendations includes seasonal influenza viruses such as A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria lineage. No specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers were reported in the supplied evidence. The recommendations are intended to guide vaccine development for the upcoming season and emphasize the importance of global solidarity in public health efforts. The WHO's Director for Epidemic and Pandemic Management, Dr Maria Van Kerhove, highlighted the long-standing effectiveness of the GISRS in informing vaccine strategies.
